query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, uniformly dispersed amount of a graphene-based reinforcer into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will foster the in situ formation of a lubricious, carbonaceous transfer film during sliding, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A coarse-grained, unreinforced CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) that, in its native form, exhibits an increasing coefficient of friction and variable wear behavior when subjected to sliding over a broad temperature range.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small weight fraction (e.g., around 0.6 wt% graphene oxide) into the HEA feedstock prior to consolidation (e.g., via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering) to create a composite material.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribological tests performed under dry or controlled atmospheres with variable loads, across temperatures ranging from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The dispersion of graphene within the alloy matrix fosters grain refinement and, importantly, forms a continuous or semi‐continuous lubricating carbonaceous layer on the sliding interface during wear.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the layered structure of graphene promotes shear slip along the basal planes, yielding a lubricious transfer film that reduces interfacial shear stresses. Additionally, its presence can lead to microstructural refinement (grain boundary strengthening) that helps accommodate stress and delays wear-related damage, thus stabilizing both friction and wear behavior over wide temperature and load ranges.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the graphene-reinforced composite is expected to show a markedly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate throughout the temperature range, with the lubricating film mitigating the usual increase in friction at intermediate temperatures.
generation.baseline: The unreinforced CoCrFeNi HEA matrix, which typically suffers from high friction variability and accelerated wear under sliding conditions as temperature, load, or environmental factors change.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to function effectively under conditions of dry or controlled-atmosphere sliding up to 800 °C and moderate-to-high loads; performance may be compromised under very aggressive oxidizing atmospheres or extreme loads that could oxidize the graphene or overwhelm its lubricating effects.
generation.uncertainty: The high-temperature (near 800 °C) oxidation stability of graphene within the alloy and its long-term retention at the sliding interface remain uncertain; further optimization of graphene content and processing parameters may be required to consistently achieve the desired tribological properties across all conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of unreinforced CoCrFeNi HEA and one set containing ~0.6 wt% graphene oxide incorporated during powder processing. Consolidate both sets under identical spark plasma sintering conditions. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests under dry (or controlled) atmosphere over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C while applying identical loads.
measurements: Real-time friction coefficient monitoring during sliding tests across the temperature range
Wear rate determination via mass loss and worn track volume measurements
Post-test microstructural evaluation (SEM/TEM) to assess the formation and integrity of a lubricating graphene-derived transfer film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-reinforced samples do not consistently exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate (beyond experimental uncertainty) compared to the unreinforced baseline across the majority of the temperature range, and if no uniform lubricating carbonaceous film is observed on the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature.
